claim: All tested cell types released multivesicular large EVs (MV-lEVs).
source: We found that all cell types we studied (including different cell lines and cells in their original tissue environment) released multivesicular large EVs (MV-lEVs).
evidence: The manuscript presents transmission electron microscopy images showing MV-lEVs in multiple cell types (HEK293T-PalmGFP, HEK293, HepG2, HT29, HL1, BMMCs, mouse kidney, and mouse liver).

claim: Upon spontaneous rupture of the limiting membrane of MV-lEVs, their intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) escaped to the extracellular environment by a 'torn bag mechanism'.
source: We also demonstrated that upon spontaneous rupture of the limiting membrane of the MV-lEVs, their intraluminal vesicles (ILVs) escaped to the extracellular environment by a 'torn bag mechanism'.
evidence: The manuscript provides TEM images showing ruptured MV-lEVs with escaping ILVs (Figure 1O-U, V) and live-cell imaging data showing the release process within 5 minutes.

claim: MV-lEVs were released by ectocytosis of amphisomes.
source: We proved that the MV-lEVs were released by ectocytosis of amphisomes (hence, we termed them amphiectosomes).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunogold TEM showing both CD63 and LC3B positive ILVs within the same MV-lEV, indicating amphisome origin, and confocal microscopy showing budding from the cell surface.

claim: ILVs of amphiectosomes and small EVs separated from conditioned media were either exclusively CD63 or LC3B positive.
source: Both ILVs of amphiectosomes and small EVs separated from conditioned media were either exclusively CD63 or LC3B positive.
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy and immunogold TEM data showing that CD63 and LC3B signals do not co-localize on individual ILVs or sEVs.

claim: Upon fusion of multivesicular bodies with autophagosomes, fragments of the autophagosomal inner membrane curl up to form LC3B positive ILVs of amphisomes.
source: According to our model, upon fusion of multivesicular bodies with autophagosomes, fragments of the autophagosomal inner membrane curl up to form LC3B positive ILVs of amphisomes, while CD63 positive small EVs are of multivesicular body origin.
evidence: The manuscript presents STED microscopy images showing the fragmentation of LC3B positive membrane and ILV formation, and immunogold TEM showing LC3B positive ILVs in amphisomes.

claim: CD63 positive small EVs are of multivesicular body origin.
source: According to our model, upon fusion of multivesicular bodies with autophagosomes, fragments of the autophagosomal inner membrane curl up to form LC3B positive ILVs of amphisomes, while CD63 positive small EVs are of multivesicular body origin.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunogold TEM showing CD63 positive ILVs in MVBs and amphisomes, and CD63 positive sEVs in conditioned medium.

claim: The 'torn bag mechanism' is a novel common release mechanism for small EVs, distinct from the exocytosis of multivesicular bodies or amphisomes.
source: Our data suggest a novel common release mechanism for small EVs, distinct from the exocytosis of multivesicular bodies or amphisomes, as well as the small ectosome release pathway.
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM and live-cell imaging data showing the rupture of MV-lEVs and release of ILVs, which differs from previously described mechanisms.

claim: The 'torn bag mechanism' is distinct from the small ectosome release pathway.
source: Our data suggest a novel common release mechanism for small EVs, distinct from the exocytosis of multivesicular bodies or amphisomes, as well as the small ectosome release pathway.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that the released sEVs originate from intracellular ILVs rather than direct budding from the plasma membrane.

claim: Human colorectal cancer cells release large, MVB-like sEV clusters en bloc in vivo.
source: The current study was prompted by our recent data showing the in vivo en bloc release of large, MVB-like sEV clusters by human colorectal cancer cells (Valcz et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication (Valcz et al., 2019) as the source of this observation.

claim: Regulatory interactions have been shown between autophagy-related molecules and EV biogenesis.
source: Recently, regulatory interactions have been shown between autophagy-related molecules and EV biogenesis (Guo et al., 2017; Murrow et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites two publications (Guo et al., 2017; Murrow et al., 2015) as evidence for this claim.

claim: The LC3-conjugation machinery specifies the cargo packaged into EVs.
source: Furthermore, the LC3-conjugation machinery was demonstrated to specify the cargo packaged into EVs (Leidal et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript cites a publication (Leidal et al., 2020) as evidence for this claim.

claim: LC3-carrying exosomes have been reported to be secreted.
source: Importantly, both others and we reported the secretion of LC3-carrying exosomes (Leidal et al., 2020; Minakaki et al., 2018).
evidence: The manuscript cites two publications (Leidal et al., 2020; Minakaki et al., 2018) as evidence for this claim.

claim: Amphisomes are hybrid organelles formed by the fusion of late endosomes/multivesicular bodies (MVBs) with autophagosomes.
source: Particularly relevant to the findings presented here is the implication of amphisomes hybrid organelles formed by the fusion of late endosomes/multivesicular bodies (MVBs) with autophagosomes (Berg et al., 1998; Fader et al., 2008) in EV biogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript cites two publications (Berg et al., 1998; Fader et al., 2008) as evidence for this definition.

claim: Fusion of the limiting membrane of amphisomes with the plasma membrane of cells results in a subsequent release of exosomes by exocytosis.
source: It was suggested that fusion of the limiting membrane of amphisomes with the plasma membrane of cells results in a subsequent release of exosomes by exocytosis (Buzas, 2023; Théry et al., 2018; Jeppesen et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites three publications (Buzas, 2023; Théry et al., 2018; Jeppesen et al., 2019) as evidence for this previously suggested mechanism.

claim: Budding of MV-lEVs carrying ILVs was detected in all tested cell types.
source: By the analysis of transmission electron micrographs of all tested cell types, we identified budding (Figure 1A–G) and secretion (Figure 1H–N) of MV-lEVs carrying ILVs.
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM images in Figure 1A-G showing budding MV-lEVs in multiple cell types.

claim: Secretion of MV-lEVs carrying ILVs was detected in all tested cell types.
source: By the analysis of transmission electron micrographs of all tested cell types, we identified budding (Figure 1A–G) and secretion (Figure 1H–N) of MV-lEVs carrying ILVs.
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM images in Figure 1H-N showing secreted MV-lEVs in multiple cell types.

claim: Evidence for the extracellular rupture of the limiting membrane of MV-lEVs and the release of ILVs was found in all tested cell types.
source: Importantly, in all cases we found evidence for the extracellular rupture of the limiting membrane of MV-lEVs and the release of ILVs (Figure 1O–U).
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM images in Figure 1O-U showing ruptured MV-lEVs with escaping ILVs in multiple cell types.

claim: The 'torn bag mechanism' is distinct from the exocytosis of MVBs and amphisomes.
source: For this novel type of sEV release, we suggest the designation 'torn bag mechanism', which is distinct from the exocytosis of MVBs and amphisomes (Buzas, 2023; Théry et al., 2018; Welsh et al., 2024; Jeppesen et al., 2019) and from the release of plasma membrane-derived sEVs by ectocytosis (Mathieu et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing a different mechanism (rupture of MV-lEVs) compared to previously described exocytosis mechanisms cited in the literature.

claim: The 'torn bag mechanism' is distinct from the release of plasma membrane-derived sEVs by ectocytosis.
source: For this novel type of sEV release, we suggest the designation 'torn bag mechanism', which is distinct from the exocytosis of MVBs and amphisomes (Buzas, 2023; Théry et al., 2018; Welsh et al., 2024; Jeppesen et al., 2019) and from the release of plasma membrane-derived sEVs by ectocytosis (Mathieu et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that the released sEVs originate from intracellular ILVs rather than direct budding from the plasma membrane, as cited in Mathieu et al., 2021.

claim: The same phenomenon of MV-lEV release and 'torn bag mechanism' was observed within ultrathin sections of murine kidney.
source: Most relevant to the in vivo conditions, we also observed the same phenomenon within the ultrathin sections of both murine kidney (Figure 1V) and liver (Figure 1W and X).
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM images in Figure 1V showing MV-lEVs and 'torn bag release' in mouse kidney tissue.

claim: The same phenomenon of MV-lEV release and 'torn bag mechanism' was observed within ultrathin sections of murine liver.
source: Most relevant to the in vivo conditions, we also observed the same phenomenon within the ultrathin sections of both murine kidney (Figure 1V) and liver (Figure 1W and X).
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM images in Figure 1W and X showing MV-lEVs and 'torn bag release' in mouse liver tissue.

claim: Both intact MV-lEVs and the 'torn bag release' of sEVs were detected in murine kidney.
source: In these cases, both the intact MV-lEVs (Figure 1V–X) and the 'torn bag release' of sEVs (Figure 1V) were detected.
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM images in Figure 1V showing both intact MV-lEVs and ruptured MV-lEVs releasing sEVs in mouse kidney.

claim: A circulating leukocyte releases MV-lEVs by ectocytosis.
source: Figure 1X shows that a circulating leukocyte releases MV-lEVs by ectocytosis.
evidence: The manuscript presents a TEM image in Figure 1X showing a leukocyte releasing MV-lEVs.

claim: MV-lEVs, lEVs, and sEVs were captured simultaneously in both kidney and liver.
source: In Figure 1—figure supplement 1, MV-lEVs, lEVs, and sEVs were captured simultaneously in both kidney (Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and D) and liver (Figure 1—figure supplement 1F, H, I).
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM images in Figure 1—figure supplement 1 showing different types of EVs present together in tissue sections.

claim: MV-lEV secretion by both endothelial and subendothelial cells can be detected in mouse liver sections.
source: In the mouse liver section (Figure 1—figure supplement 1G), MV-lEV secretion by both endothelial and subendothelial cells can be detected.
evidence: The manuscript presents a TEM image in Figure 1—figure supplement 1G showing MV-lEV secretion by different cell types in liver tissue.

claim: Several micrographs suggested an at least partially intact double membrane of MV-lEVs.
source: However, several micrographs suggested an at least partially intact double membrane (Figure 1Y-AF) of MV-lEVs.
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM images in Figure 1Y-AF showing MV-lEVs with apparent double membrane structures.

claim: In BMMCs, the bottom portion of a releasing multivesicular structure embedded in the cytoplasm is surrounded by a single membrane while the upper (budding) portion is covered by double membrane.
source: In the case of BMMCs (Figure 1Y), the release phase of a multivesicular structure is captured. The bottom portion of this structure, embedded in the cytoplasm, is surrounded by a single membrane while the upper (budding) portion is covered by double membrane.
evidence: The manuscript presents a TEM image in Figure 1Y showing a BMMC with a budding MV-lEV with different membrane structures.

claim: Disruption of the original amphisome membrane mainly occurs after separation of the MV-lEV from the cell to avoid the release of ILVs inside the cell.
source: We hypothesize that disruption of the original amphisome membrane mainly occurs after separation of the MV-lEV from the cell to avoid the release of ILVs inside the cell.
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM images showing intact double membranes during budding and ruptured membranes after release, supporting this hypothesis.

claim: The PalmGFP signal of HEK293T-PalmGFP cells principally associates with the plasma membrane.
source: The PalmGFP signal of HEK293T-PalmGFP cells principally associates with the plasma membrane (Kovács et al., 2023; Figure 2—figure supplement 1A–C), therefore the green fluorescence helped us to identify the plasma membrane-derived limiting membrane of MV-lEVs.
evidence: The manuscript cites a previous publication (Kovács et al., 2023) and presents immunofluorescence data in Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C showing PalmGFP localization.

claim: Within MV-lEVs, CD63/ALIX double positive ILVs or ILV clusters were found.
source: In agreement with our previous findings on HT29 colorectal cancer cells, within the MV-lEVs, we found CD63/ALIX (Figure 2A and G), CD81/ALIX (Figure 2B and H), CD63/TSG101 (Figure 2C and I), and CD81/TSG101 (Figure 2D and J) double positive ILVs or ILV clusters.
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy images in Figure 2A and G showing co-localization of CD63 and ALIX in ILVs.

claim: Within MV-lEVs, CD81/ALIX double positive ILVs or ILV clusters were found.
source: In agreement with our previous findings on HT29 colorectal cancer cells, within the MV-lEVs, we found CD63/ALIX (Figure 2A and G), CD81/ALIX (Figure 2B and H), CD63/TSG101 (Figure 2C and I), and CD81/TSG101 (Figure 2D and J) double positive ILVs or ILV clusters.
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy images in Figure 2B and H showing co-localization of CD81 and ALIX in ILVs.

claim: Within MV-lEVs, CD63/TSG101 double positive ILVs or ILV clusters were found.
source: In agreement with our previous findings on HT29 colorectal cancer cells, within the MV-lEVs, we found CD63/ALIX (Figure 2A and G), CD81/ALIX (Figure 2B and H), CD63/TSG101 (Figure 2C and I), and CD81/TSG101 (Figure 2D and J) double positive ILVs or ILV clusters.
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy images in Figure 2C and I showing co-localization of CD63 and TSG101 in ILVs.

claim: Within MV-lEVs, CD81/TSG101 double positive ILVs or ILV clusters were found.
source: In agreement with our previous findings on HT29 colorectal cancer cells, within the MV-lEVs, we found CD63/ALIX (Figure 2A and G), CD81/ALIX (Figure 2B and H), CD63/TSG101 (Figure 2C and I), and CD81/TSG101 (Figure 2D and J) double positive ILVs or ILV clusters.
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy images in Figure 2D and J showing co-localization of CD81 and TSG101 in ILVs.

claim: LC3B, CD63, and CD81 were all present in association with the ILVs.
source: Although LC3B, CD63, and CD81 were all present in association with the ILVs (Figure 2E and F), the LC3B and CD63 (Figure 2K) and the LC3B and CD81 (Figure 2L) signals did not overlap.
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy images in Figure 2E and F showing the presence of all three markers in ILVs.

claim: The LC3B and CD63 signals did not overlap in ILVs.
source: Although LC3B, CD63, and CD81 were all present in association with the ILVs (Figure 2E and F), the LC3B and CD63 (Figure 2K) and the LC3B and CD81 (Figure 2L) signals did not overlap.
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy images and co-localization analysis in Figure 2K showing lack of overlap between LC3B and CD63.

claim: The LC3B and CD81 signals did not overlap in ILVs.
source: Although LC3B, CD63, and CD81 were all present in association with the ILVs (Figure 2E and F), the LC3B and CD63 (Figure 2K) and the LC3B and CD81 (Figure 2L) signals did not overlap.
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy images and co-localization analysis in Figure 2L showing lack of overlap between LC3B and CD81.

claim: Known sEV markers (CD63, CD81, TSG101, and ALIX) strongly co-localized with each other.
source: Figure 2M shows that while the known sEV markers (CD63, CD81, TSG101, and ALIX) strongly co-localized with each other, LC3B positivity hardly showed co-localization with CD63 or CD81.
evidence: The manuscript presents co-localization analysis in Figure 2M showing high co-localization rates among conventional sEV markers.

claim: LC3B positivity hardly showed co-localization with CD63 or CD81.
source: Figure 2M shows that while the known sEV markers (CD63, CD81, TSG101, and ALIX) strongly co-localized with each other, LC3B positivity hardly showed co-localization with CD63 or CD81.
evidence: The manuscript presents co-localization analysis in Figure 2M showing low co-localization rates between LC3B and conventional sEV markers.

claim: The ILVs of HEK293T-PalmGFP and HepG2 cell lines were Rab7 positive.
source: The ILVs of HEK293T-PalmGFP and HepG2 cell lines were also Rab7 positive (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B), suggesting a late endosomal origin.
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy images in Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B showing Rab7 positivity in ILVs.

claim: Rab7 positivity of ILVs suggests a late endosomal origin.
source: The ILVs of HEK293T-PalmGFP and HepG2 cell lines were also Rab7 positive (Figure 2—figure supplement 3A and B), suggesting a late endosomal origin.
evidence: Rab7 is a well-established marker of late endosomes, and its presence on ILVs supports their late endosomal origin.

claim: Distinct LC3B positive and CD63 positive sEVs were found using TEM double immunogold labeling.
source: With TEM double immunogold labeling, using anti-LC3B and anti-CD63 antibodies simultaneously, we found distinct LC3B positive (Figure 2Q, Figure 2—figure supplement 6O) and CD63 positive (Figure 2R, Figure 2—figure supplement 6O) sEVs.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunogold TEM images in Figure 2Q and R showing separate populations of LC3B and CD63 positive sEVs.

claim: LC3B positive sEVs had a significantly larger diameter compared to LC3B negative ones.
source: The LC3B positive sEVs had a significantly larger diameter as compared to the LC3B negative ones.
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative analysis in Figure 2S showing statistically significant size differences between LC3B positive and negative sEVs.

claim: The 'torn bag mechanism' was monitored by live-cell SIM2 super-resolution microscopy analysis of HEK293T-PalmGFP-LC3RFP cells.
source: The 'torn bag mechanism' was also monitored by live-cell SIM2 super-resolution microscopy analysis of HEK293T-PalmGFP-LC3RFP cells (Figure 2N and O).
evidence: The manuscript presents live-cell imaging data in Figure 2N and O showing the release of LC3 positive sEVs from amphiectosomes.

claim: The release of LC3 positive red fluorescent signal was detected within a relatively short period of time (the first LC3 positive ILVs left the amphiectosome within 40 s, the whole 'torn bag' sEV release process was completed within 260 s).
source: The release of the LC3 positive red fluorescent signal was detected within a relatively short period of time (the first LC3 positive ILVs left the amphiectosome within 40 s, the whole 'torn bag' sEV release process was completed within 260 s) (Figure 2O).
evidence: The manuscript presents time-lapse imaging data in Figure 2O showing the temporal dynamics of the 'torn bag' release process.

claim: Rupture of the limiting membrane detected by TEM was not a fixation artifact.
source: We could rule out the possibility that rupture of the limiting membrane detected by TEM (Figure 1O–T, V) was a fixation artifact by showing the spontaneous release of LC3 positive sEVs from amphiectosomes with live-cell imaging.
evidence: The manuscript presents live-cell imaging data showing the same rupture phenomenon observed in fixed samples, ruling out fixation artifacts.

claim: CD63 single positivity was found in MVBs using immune electron microscopy.
source: Using immune electron microscopy, as expected, we found CD63 single positivity in MVBs (Figure 2—figure supplement 6K).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunogold TEM images in Figure 2—figure supplement 6K showing CD63 but not LC3B in MVBs.

claim: In autophagosomes, the limiting phagophore membrane was LC3B positive, and CD63 positivity was also present.
source: In autophagosomes, the limiting phagophore membrane was LC3B positive, and CD63 positivity was also present (Figure 2—figure supplement 6L).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunogold TEM images in Figure 2—figure supplement 6L showing both LC3B and CD63 in autophagosomes.

claim: The limiting membrane of amphisomes was LC3B negative, and the internal membranous structures were either LC3B or CD63 positive.
source: The limiting membrane of amphisomes was LC3B negative, and the internal membranous structures were either LC3B or CD63 positive (Figure 2—figure supplement 6M).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunogold TEM images in Figure 2—figure supplement 6M showing the distribution of LC3B and CD63 in amphisomes.

claim: The same immunoreactivity observed in amphisomes was also observed in the ILVs of the released amphiectosomes.
source: The same immunoreactivity was also observed in the ILVs of the released amphiectosomes (Figure 2—figure supplement 6N).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunogold TEM images in Figure 2—figure supplement 6N showing similar LC3B and CD63 distribution in amphiectosomes as in amphisomes.

claim: sEVs separated from serum-free conditioned medium of HEK293T-PalmGFP cells were either LC3B or CD63 positive.
source: Importantly, sEVs separated from serum-free conditioned medium of HEK293T-PalmGFP cells were either LC3B or CD63 positive (Figure 2—figure supplement 6O).
evidence: The manuscript presents immunogold TEM images in Figure 2—figure supplement 6O showing separate populations of LC3B and CD63 positive sEVs.

claim: LC3B positive ILVs had a significantly larger diameter than the LC3B negative ones.
source: In agreement with our observations with separated sEVs, LC3B positive ILVs had a significantly larger diameter than the LC3B negative ones (Figure 2—figure supplement 6R) possibly indicating difference in membrane composition and their different intracellular origin.
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative analysis in Figure 2—figure supplement 6R showing statistically significant size differences between LC3B positive and negative ILVs.

claim: Size differences between LC3B positive and negative ILVs possibly indicate difference in membrane composition and their different intracellular origin.
source: In agreement with our observations with separated sEVs, LC3B positive ILVs had a significantly larger diameter than the LC3B negative ones (Figure 2—figure supplement 6R) possibly indicating difference in membrane composition and their different intracellular origin.
evidence: The manuscript presents size data and proposes an interpretation based on known differences in membrane composition between autophagosomes and MVBs.

claim: Autophagosomes and MVBs fuse to form amphisomes.
source: Based on all the above findings, we propose the following model (Figure 3A): autophagosomes and MVBs fuse to form amphisomes, and the inner, LC3 positive membrane of autophagosomes undergoes fragmentation (Klionsky, 2021).
evidence: The manuscript presents a model in Figure 3A based on the experimental data and cites a reference (Klionsky, 2021) for the fragmentation process.

claim: The inner, LC3 positive membrane of autophagosomes undergoes fragmentation.
source: Based on all the above findings, we propose the following model (Figure 3A): autophagosomes and MVBs fuse to form amphisomes, and the inner, LC3 positive membrane of autophagosomes undergoes fragmentation (Klionsky, 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference (Klionsky, 2021) for the fragmentation process and presents STED microscopy images showing fragmentation.

claim: Membrane fragments curl up and form LC3 positive ILVs.
source: Membrane fragments curl up and form LC3 positive ILVs.
evidence: The manuscript presents STED microscopy images in Figure 3F showing the formation of LC3 positive ILVs from membrane fragments.

claim: Amphisomes contain both MVB-derived CD63 positive/LC3 negative and autophagosome-derived, CD63 negative/LC3 positive ILVs.
source: Therefore, amphisomes contain both MVB-derived CD63 positive/LC3 negative and autophagosome-derived, CD63 negative/LC3 positive ILVs.
evidence: The manuscript presents immunogold TEM images showing both CD63 positive and LC3B positive ILVs within the same amphisome.

claim: The amphisome is released from the cell by ectocytosis.
source: The amphisome is next released from the cell by ectocytosis.
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM images showing budding of amphisomes from the cell surface.

claim: The plasma membrane-derived outer membrane ruptures enabling the ILVs escape to the extracellular space by a 'torn bag mechanism'.
source: Finally, the plasma membrane-derived outer membrane ruptures enabling the ILVs escape to the extracellular space by a 'torn bag mechanism'.
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM and live-cell imaging data showing rupture of the outer membrane and release of ILVs.

claim: The intracellular phases of the proposed model were documented using STED microscopy: MVB, autophagosome, fusion of MVB and autophagosome, fragmentation of the LC3 positive membrane and ILV formation from the membrane fragments, and mature amphisome.
source: By using stimulated emission depletion (STED) microscopy, we documented the intracellular phases of our proposed model: MVB (Figure 3B), autophagosome (Figure 3D), the fusion of MVB and autophagosome (Figure 3C), fragmentation of the LC3 positive membrane and ILV formation from the membrane fragments (Figure 3F) and mature amphisome (Figure 3E).
evidence: The manuscript presents STED microscopy images in Figure 3B-F showing different stages of amphisome formation.

claim: The plasma membrane origin of the external membrane of amphiectosome was supported by wheat germ agglutinin (WGA)-based live-cell labeling.
source: The plasma membrane origin of the external membrane of amphiectosome was further supported by wheat germ agglutinin (WGA)-based live-cell labeling (Figure 3G).
evidence: The manuscript presents live-cell imaging data in Figure 3G showing WGA labeling of the external membrane of budding amphiectosomes.

claim: Cytochalasin B did not alter the dynamics of amphiectosome release.
source: Based on confocal microscopy, Cytochalasin B (CytoB) did not alter the dynamics of amphiectosome release (I).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative confocal microscopy data in Figure 3I showing no significant change in amphiectosome release with Cytochalasin B treatment.

claim: Cytochalasin B did not have any effect on the discharge of MV-lEVs suggesting that the release did not involve a major actin-dependent mechanism.
source: Cytochalasin B did not have any effect on the discharge of MV-lEVs suggesting that the release did not involve a major actin-dependent mechanism.
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data showing no effect of Cytochalasin B (an actin polymerization inhibitor) on MV-lEV release.

claim: Colchicine significantly inhibited the release of amphiectosomes.
source: In contrast, both Colchicine (Colch) and Rapamycin (Rapa) significantly inhibited the release of amphiectosomes, while Chloroquine (Chloro) and Bafilomycin (Bafilo) increased the release frequency.
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative confocal microscopy data in Figure 3I showing significant reduction in amphiectosome release with Colchicine treatment.

claim: There was a significant reduction of the MV-lEV secretion upon exposure of the cells to Colchicine indicating a role of microtubules in the release of the MV-lEVs.
source: In contrast, there was a significant reduction of the MV-lEV secretion upon exposure of the cells to Colchicine indicating a role of microtubules in the release of the MV-lEVs.
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative data showing reduced MV-lEV release with Colchicine (a microtubule inhibitor) treatment.

claim: Rapamycin significantly inhibited the release of amphiectosomes.
source: In contrast, both Colchicine (Colch) and Rapamycin (Rapa) significantly inhibited the release of amphiectosomes, while Chloroquine (Chloro) and Bafilomycin (Bafilo) increased the release frequency.
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative confocal microscopy data in Figure 3I showing significant reduction in amphiectosome release with Rapamycin treatment.

claim: Rapamycin significantly reduced the discharge of MV-lEVs.
source: While Rapamycin significantly reduced the discharge of MV-lEVs, Chloroquine and Bafilomycin induced an enhanced MV-lEV secretion.
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative confocal microscopy data in Figure 3I showing significant reduction in MV-lEV release with Rapamycin treatment.

claim: Rapamycin activates autophagic degradation.
source: Rapamycin activates autophagic degradation (Xie et al., 2021), therefore, it induces a shift toward degradation as opposed to secretion.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference (Xie et al., 2021) for the effect of Rapamycin on autophagy.

claim: Rapamycin induces a shift toward degradation as opposed to secretion.
source: Rapamycin activates autophagic degradation (Xie et al., 2021), therefore, it induces a shift toward degradation as opposed to secretion.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing reduced amphiectosome release with Rapamycin treatment and cites literature on Rapamycin's effect on autophagy.

claim: Chloroquine increased the release frequency of amphiectosomes.
source: In contrast, both Colchicine (Colch) and Rapamycin (Rapa) significantly inhibited the release of amphiectosomes, while Chloroquine (Chloro) and Bafilomycin (Bafilo) increased the release frequency.
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative confocal microscopy data in Figure 3I showing increased amphiectosome release with Chloroquine treatment.

claim: Bafilomycin increased the release frequency of amphiectosomes.
source: In contrast, both Colchicine (Colch) and Rapamycin (Rapa) significantly inhibited the release of amphiectosomes, while Chloroquine (Chloro) and Bafilomycin (Bafilo) increased the release frequency.
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative confocal microscopy data in Figure 3I showing increased amphiectosome release with Bafilomycin treatment.

claim: Chloroquine and Bafilomycin induced an enhanced MV-lEV secretion.
source: While Rapamycin significantly reduced the discharge of MV-lEVs, Chloroquine and Bafilomycin induced an enhanced MV-lEV secretion.
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative confocal microscopy data in Figure 3I showing increased MV-lEV release with Chloroquine and Bafilomycin treatment.

claim: There was no difference between the effect of Chloroquine and Bafilomycin on amphiectosome release.
source: There was no difference between the effect of Chloroquine and Bafilomycin (I).
evidence: The manuscript presents quantitative confocal microscopy data in Figure 3I showing similar effects of Chloroquine and Bafilomycin on amphiectosome release.

claim: Chloroquine and Bafilomycin are known to interfere with the acidification of lysosomes.
source: The lysosomotropic agents Chloroquine and Bafilomycin are known to interfere with the acidification of lysosomes (Chen et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites two references (Chen et al., 2011; Wang et al., 2021) for the effect of these agents on lysosomal acidification.

claim: By blocking the degradation pathway of MVBs/amphisomes, an enhanced sEV secretion is observed.
source: By blocking the degradation pathway of MVBs/amphisomes (Figure 3H), an enhanced sEV secretion is observed.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing increased amphiectosome release with Chloroquine and Bafilomycin treatment, which block lysosomal degradation.

claim: This effect is well known for exosome secretion from MVBs.
source: This effect is well known for exosome secretion from MVBs (Edgar et al., 2016; Ortega et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites two references (Edgar et al., 2016; Ortega et al., 2019) for the known effect of blocking degradation on exosome secretion.

claim: A significant reduction in metabolic activity was detected upon exposure of the cells to Rapamycin.
source: Metabolic activity of the cells was determined by a Resazurin assay, and a significant reduction was detected upon exposure of the cells to Rapamycin (Figure 3—figure supplement 1D) in line with previously published data (Zhang et al., 2020).
evidence: The manuscript presents Resazurin assay data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1D showing reduced metabolic activity with Rapamycin treatment.

claim: LC3II is the membrane-associated, lipidated autophagic form of LC3.
source: LC3II is the membrane-associated, lipidated autophagic form of LC3 (Tanida et al., 2008) and it is the hallmark of autophagy-related membranes (Klionsky, 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites two references (Tanida et al., 2008; Klionsky, 2021) for the definition and significance of LC3II.

claim: LC3II is the hallmark of autophagy-related membranes.
source: LC3II is the membrane-associated, lipidated autophagic form of LC3 (Tanida et al., 2008) and it is the hallmark of autophagy-related membranes (Klionsky, 2021).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference (Klionsky, 2021) for LC3II as a hallmark of autophagy-related membranes.

claim: Membrane-bound LC3II was present in serum-free, lEV-depleted (sEV containing) conditioned medium of both HEK293T-PalmGFP and HEK293T-PalmGFP-LC3RFP cells.
source: Importantly, by western blot, we not only showed the presence of the membrane-bound LC3II in serum-free, lEV-depleted (sEV containing) conditioned medium of both HEK293T-PalmGFP and HEK293T-PalmGFP-LC3RFP cells, but the amount of LC3II substantially increased upon Chloroquine treatment (Figure 3J).
evidence: The manuscript presents western blot data in Figure 3J showing LC3II bands in conditioned medium.

claim: The amount of LC3II substantially increased upon Chloroquine treatment.
source: Importantly, by western blot, we not only showed the presence of the membrane-bound LC3II in serum-free, lEV-depleted (sEV containing) conditioned medium of both HEK293T-PalmGFP and HEK293T-PalmGFP-LC3RFP cells, but the amount of LC3II substantially increased upon Chloroquine treatment (Figure 3J).
evidence: The manuscript presents western blot data in Figure 3J showing increased LC3II levels with Chloroquine treatment.

claim: Chloroquine treatment increased the LC3II level by approximately twofold.
source: Chloroquine treatment increased the LC3II level by approximately twofold.
evidence: The manuscript presents densitometry analysis of western blot data showing approximately twofold increase in LC3II with Chloroquine treatment.

claim: Migrasomes are a special type of MV-lEVs.
source: Recent advances in the EV field shed light on migrasomes, a special type of MV-lEVs (Liang et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2015).
evidence: The manuscript cites two references (Liang et al., 2023; Ma et al., 2015) for the definition of migrasomes.

claim: With their pomegranate-like ultrastructure, migrasomes resemble amphiectosomes.
source: With their pomegranate-like ultrastructure, migrasomes resemble amphiectosomes.
evidence: The manuscript compares the ultrastructure of migrasomes (from literature) with the observed amphiectosomes.

claim: TSPAN4 is a migrasome limiting membrane marker.
source: Therefore, we tested the presence of TSPAN4, a migrasome limiting membrane marker (Ma et al., 2015), in amphiectosomes.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference (Ma et al., 2015) for TSPAN4 as a migrasome marker.

claim: TSPAN4 was present intraluminally in the HEK293T-PalmGFP-derived MV-lEVs, but was clearly absent from their external membrane.
source: Figure 4A, B, G, and H shows that although TSPAN4 was present intraluminally in the HEK293T-PalmGFP-derived MV-lEVs, it was clearly absent from their external membrane.
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy images in Figure 4A, B, G, and H showing TSPAN4 localization in HEK293T-PalmGFP-derived MV-lEVs.

claim: Two different HT29 cell-derived MV-lEV populations were identified: one in which TSPAN4 was only located intraluminally, and another one with a TSPAN4 positive external membrane.
source: Surprisingly, we identified two different HT29 cell-derived MV-lEV populations: one in which TSPAN4 was only located intraluminally (Figure 4C, E, I, and K), and another one with a TSPAN4 positive external membrane (Figure 4D, F, J, and L).
evidence: The manuscript presents confocal microscopy images in Figure 4C-F and I-L showing two distinct populations of HT29-derived MV-lEVs with different TSPAN4 localization.

claim: The HT29 cell-derived MV-lEV population with a TSPAN4 positive external membrane corresponds to migrasomes.
source: This raised the possibility that the latter population corresponded to migrasomes.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing TSPAN4 on the external membrane of some HT29-derived MV-lEVs, which is consistent with the migrasome marker pattern.

claim: The released MV-lEVs were either LC3 positive or negative intraluminally.
source: Next, we carried out live-cell imaging on HEK293T-PalmGFP-LC3RFP cells. The released MV-lEVs were either LC3 positive or negative intraluminally (Figure 4N and O).
evidence: The manuscript presents live-cell imaging data in Figure 4N and O showing MV-lEVs with and without intraluminal LC3 positivity.

claim: Certain cell types can release both migrasome-like structures and amphiectosomes.
source: Our TEM images confirmed that certain cell types can release both migrasome-like structures and amphiectosomes.
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM images showing both retraction fiber-associated MV-lEVs (migrasome-like) and budding amphiectosomes from the same cell types.

claim: MV-lEVs with typical migrasome-associated retraction fiber(s) were detected in HL1, HEK293T-PalmGFP, and BMMC cells.
source: MV-lEVs with typical migrasome-associated retraction fiber(s) were detected in the case of HL1 (Figure 4P), HEK293T-PalmGFP (Figure 4Q), and BMMC cells (Figure 4R).
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM images in Figure 4P-R showing MV-lEVs associated with retraction fibers in multiple cell types.

claim: The elongated structures observed may correspond to tunnelling nanotubes.
source: Of note, it cannot be excluded that the elongated structures observed in the above cases may correspond to tunnelling nanotubes (Drab et al., 2019).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference (Drab et al., 2019) and acknowledges the possibility that some observed structures might be tunnelling nanotubes.

claim: The same cell lines that released migrasome-like structures also released amphiectosomes by budding from the cell surface.
source: Importantly, the same cell lines also released amphiectosomes by budding from the cell surface (Figure 4S–U).
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM images in Figure 4S-U showing budding amphiectosomes from HL1, HEK293T-PalmGFP, and BMMC cells.

claim: Based on the absence of TSPAN4 in their external membrane, and their lack of association with retraction fibers, amphiectosomes appear to be distinct from migrasomes.
source: Taken together, based on the absence of TSPAN4 in their external membrane, and their lack of association with retraction fibers, amphiectosomes appear to be distinct from migrasomes.
evidence: The manuscript presents data showing that amphiectosomes lack TSPAN4 on their external membrane and are not associated with retraction fibers, distinguishing them from migrasomes.

claim: Another MV-lEV type was described in the case of gastrointestinal tumors and low-grade glioblastoma cells referred to as spheresome.
source: Besides migrasomes, another MV-lEV type was described in the case of gastrointestinal tumors and low-grade glioblastoma cells referred to as spheresome (Baselga et al., 2023; Junquera et al., 2016).
evidence: The manuscript cites two references (Baselga et al., 2023; Junquera et al., 2016) for the description of spheresomes.

claim: There is no data on a relationship of spheresome release and autophagy.
source: However, there is no data on a relationship of spheresome release and autophagy.
evidence: The manuscript states the absence of data linking spheresomes to autophagy in the literature.

claim: Endothelial cell-derived, multicompartmented microvesicles (MCMVs) were shown to protrude and pinch off from the cell surface releasing ILVs by a mechanism similar to exocytosis.
source: Recently, endothelial cell-derived, multicompartmented microvesicles (MCMVs) were shown to protrude and pinch off from the cell surface releasing ILVs by a mechanism similar to exocytosis (Petersen et al., 2023).
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference (Petersen et al., 2023) for the description of MCMVs.

claim: The absence of protrusion clusters described for MCMV distinguishes amphiectosomes from MCMVs.
source: The absence of protrusion clusters described for MCMV (Petersen et al., 2023) distinguishes amphiectosomes from MCMVs.
evidence: The manuscript compares amphiectosomes with MCMVs from the literature and identifies a distinguishing feature.

claim: The previously described 'nodal vesicular parcels' might be special examples of amphiectosomes.
source: In addition, the previously described so-called 'nodal vesicular parcels' (Tanaka et al., 2005) might be special examples of amphiectosomes.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference (Tanaka et al., 2005) and suggests a possible relationship between nodal vesicular parcels and amphiectosomes.

claim: In Caenorhabditis elegans, the release autophagy and stress-related large EVs (lEVs) (exophers) has been documented.
source: Finally, in Caenorhabditis elegans, the release autophagy and stress-related large EVs (lEVs) (exophers) has been documented (Melentijevic et al., 2017; Cooper et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2024).
evidence: The manuscript cites three references (Melentijevic et al., 2017; Cooper et al., 2021; Yang et al., 2024) for the description of exophers.

claim: Exophers contain damaged organelles and do not have an MV-lEV-like ultrastructure.
source: They contain damaged organelles and do not have an MV-lEV-like ultrastructure.
evidence: The manuscript describes the characteristics of exophers from the literature to distinguish them from amphiectosomes.

claim: Amphiectosomes have multivesicular structure without recognizable damaged organelles.
source: In contrast, the amphiectosomes we described here have multivesicular structure without recognizable damaged organelles.
evidence: The manuscript presents TEM images showing the multivesicular structure of amphiectosomes without damaged organelles.

claim: The in situ fixation approach made it possible to recognize sEV release from amphiectosomes by the 'torn bag mechanism'.
source: Our approach, involving in situ fixation of cultures and tissues, made it possible to recognize sEV release from amphiectosomes by the 'torn bag mechanism'.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodological approach that enabled the discovery of the 'torn bag mechanism'.

claim: This mechanism could be easily missed earlier if conditioned medium was subjected to centrifugation, SEC purification, or even to simple pipetting, which may rupture the limiting membrane of amphiectosomes.
source: We propose that this mechanism could be easily missed earlier if conditioned medium was subjected to centrifugation, SEC purification, or even to simple pipetting, which may rupture the limiting membrane of amphiectosomes.
evidence: The manuscript proposes an explanation for why this mechanism may have been missed in previous studies using standard EV isolation methods.

claim: The spontaneous escape of ILVs from untouched amphiectosomes can be completed as early as 5 min after amphiectosome release.
source: This aligns with our observation that the spontaneous escape of ILVs from untouched amphiectosomes can be completed as early as 5 min after amphiectosome release.
evidence: The manuscript presents live-cell imaging data showing the time course of ILV release from amphiectosomes.

claim: The exocytosis of MVBs/amphisomes under steady-state conditions is rarely documented in the scientific literature.
source: Based on our data presented here, and considering that the exocytosis of MVBs/amphisomes under steady-state conditions is rarely documented in the scientific literature, we suggest that amphiectosome secretion and the 'torn bag mechanism' may have a significant, yet previously unrecognized, role in sEV biogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript reviews the literature and notes the rarity of documented MVB/amphisome exocytosis under steady-state conditions.

claim: Amphiectosome secretion and the 'torn bag mechanism' may have a significant, yet previously unrecognized, role in sEV biogenesis.
source: Based on our data presented here, and considering that the exocytosis of MVBs/amphisomes under steady-state conditions is rarely documented in the scientific literature, we suggest that amphiectosome secretion and the 'torn bag mechanism' may have a significant, yet previously unrecognized, role in sEV biogenesis.
evidence: The manuscript presents extensive data showing the 'torn bag mechanism' in multiple cell types and proposes its significance in sEV biogenesis.

claim: Serum starvation significantly affects autophagy.
source: As serum starvation significantly affects autophagy (Wang et al., 2023), and EV-depleted FBS in the cell culture medium may influence cellular physiology and morphology (Lehrich et al., 2021), FBS was not removed before fixation.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference (Wang et al., 2023) for the effect of serum starvation on autophagy.

claim: EV-depleted FBS in the cell culture medium may influence cellular physiology and morphology.
source: As serum starvation significantly affects autophagy (Wang et al., 2023), and EV-depleted FBS in the cell culture medium may influence cellular physiology and morphology (Lehrich et al., 2021), FBS was not removed before fixation.
evidence: The manuscript cites a reference (Lehrich et al., 2021) for the effect of EV-depleted FBS on cellular physiology.

claim: EVs in the size range >350–500 nm are negligible in FBS because of sterile filtration and heat inactivation of the serum.
source: Our study focuses on lEVs with diameter >350–500 nm. EVs in this size range are negligible in FBS because of sterile filtration and heat inactivation of the serum.
evidence: The manuscript explains why FBS does not interfere with the study of large EVs based on standard serum processing methods.

claim: Centrifugation may disrupt the limiting membrane of amphiectosomes.
source: Since centrifugation may disrupt the limiting membrane of amphiectosomes, the in situ fixation made it possible to observe them in their intact form.
evidence: The manuscript proposes that centrifugation could damage amphiectosomes based on their observed fragility.

claim: The released lEVs were either fixed and captured during the release or were preserved on the gelatin/fibronectin surface coating.
source: The released lEVs were either fixed and captured during the release or were preserved on the gelatin/fibronectin surface coating.
evidence: The manuscript describes the methodological approach for preserving released EVs in their original microenvironment.
